newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela prison head blames guards for fatal fire.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela prison head blames guards for fatal fire.

text.p: National Guardsmen seem to have deliberately started the fire that killed at least 25 inmates of a crowded Venezuelan jail, officials said on Wednesday.

National Prisons Director Antonio Marval said Tuesday's fire appeared to have been started on purpose by the guards, who locked a group of inmates into a small cell at La Planta prison and then lobbed in tear gas and incendiary devices.
"There were tear gas canisters and incendiary devices there," Marval told reporters outside the jail. It was not clear why the guards decided to lock up the inmates, he said.
The mother of one of the 25 victims said guards had told inmates last week they would carry out a massacre.
"He told us that they were afraid, because a guard told them he was going to burn them alive," Carmen Sanchez told Union Radio.

The guards on duty at the time of the incident were arrested and placed at the disposition of the investigating military judge, Defence Minister Pedro Valencia said. The National Guard provides additional security at Venezuela's overcrowded and violence-prone prisons.

Prisoners at the jail in the southwestern outskirts of Caracas said the fire began after an argument broke out between inmates and guards during an early-morning roll call. About 40 inmates were trapped inside the small cell.

"What happened here was murder ... There was a mountain of horribly burned bodies one on top of another, because they all died trying to reach a small gap in the roof," Aurelio Ferrin, the jail's chaplain, told Reuters.

Provea, a local human rights group, called on the government to remove the National Guard from all Venezuelan prisons and demanded that those responsible be brought to trial. Congress said it would open its own investigation.
Morgue officials said 25 charred and twisted bodies had been recovered from the jail. They said only five had been identified, because they were so badly burned.
"I knew them all. It's not fair that they suffered this punishment," Ferrin said. He added that many of the dead were accused of minor crimes and most had not been sentenced.

A Reuters photographer who entered the burned-out cell on Tuesday said several prisoners had tried to escape the flames by hiding under beds, while others had fused together from clinging to one another as they died.
About 100 tearful relatives, many of whom had camped out overnight, waited outside the jail to find out the names of the dead, turning a regular visiting day into one of mourning and tension.

"I went to identify my brother, but it's impossible. All I saw was coal. It (the body) doesn't even have hands," Carmen Luisa Alvarado said. Her brother Libio Alvarado spent a year in La Planta awaiting trial for a robbery.
"He slept in that room with about 40 people, one on top of the other, but we still don't know if he is alive or not," she said.
Inside the jail, tensions had eased, although prison officials said one inmate was taken to a hospital in the afternoon for treatment of a knife wound.
Venezuela's decaying prisons, considered among the most dangerous in Latin America, are frequent scenes of violence between inmates and clashes with guards.

The death toll at La Planta was the highest in Venezuela's jails since about 120 prisoners were burned or hacked to death with machetes during a gang fight at the Sabaneta jail in the western city of Maracaibo in January 1994.
La Planta was built for 300 prisoners but currently holds about 1,700, officials said.
